notes.front: What is AI Hypercomputer?
notes.back: Google Cloud’s integrated supercomputing system for artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning workloads: the unified portfolio of its AI infrastructure.
notes.explanation: It is a single entry point for exploring, configuring and deploying performance-optimised hardware, open software and flexible consumption models.
notes.example: Like one showroom for a racing team: the engines, the tuning software and the ways to hire the car are all found in one place.
notes.evidence: AI Hypercomputer is an integrated supercomputing system that's optimized to support your artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) workloads. It is the unified portfolio for Google Cloud's AI infrastructure, and provides a single entry point to explore, configure, and deploy performance-optimized hardware, open software, and flexible consumption models.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, AI Hypercomputer overview, “AI Hypercomputer overview”

notes.front: What is a Tensor Processing Unit (TPU)?
notes.back: Tensor Processing Unit (TPU): a Google custom-developed, application-specific integrated circuit that accelerates machine learning workloads.
notes.explanation: Its hardware is designed for the large matrix operations often found in machine learning algorithms.
notes.example: Like a calculator built only for multiplying huge tables of numbers: superb at that one job, less flexible at others.
notes.evidence: Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) are Google's custom-developed, application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) used to accelerate machine learning workloads. For more information about TPU hardware, see TPU architecture. TPUs efficiently train your models by using hardware designed for performing large matrix operations often found in machine learning algorithms.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Introduction to Cloud TPU, “Introduction to Cloud TPU”

notes.front: What is a GPU machine type on Compute Engine?
notes.back: A machine type with Nvidia GPUs to accelerate machine learning, data processing and graphics-intensive workloads.
notes.explanation: Accelerator-optimised series come with GPUs pre-attached, and some general-purpose instances let you attach GPUs yourself.
notes.example: Like hiring a van with the tow bar already fitted, rather than bolting one onto your own car.
notes.evidence: This document outlines the NVIDIA GPU models that you can use to accelerate machine learning (ML), data processing, and graphics-intensive workloads on your Compute Engine instances. This document also details which GPUs come pre-attached to accelerator-optimized machine series such as A4X Max, A4X, A4, A3, A2, G4, and G2, and which GPUs you can attach to N1 general-purpose instances.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, GPU machine types (Compute Engine), “GPU machine types”

notes.front: What is Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform?
notes.back: Google Cloud’s platform for building, scaling, governing and optimising enterprise-grade AI agents grounded in enterprise data.
notes.explanation: It provides the full-stack foundation for turning applications and workflows into reliable agentic systems at global scale.
notes.example: Like a workshop with every tool needed to make, run and supervise a company’s digital assistants.
notes.evidence: Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform is our open and comprehensive platform that empowers businesses to rapidly build, scale, govern, and optimize enterprise-grade agents grounded in your enterprise data. It provides the full-stack foundation and extensive developer choice you need to transform your applications and workflows into powerful, reliable agentic systems at global scale.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, “Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform”

notes.front: What is Agent Platform Pipelines?
notes.back: A service that automates, monitors and governs machine learning systems serverlessly, using pipelines to orchestrate machine learning workflows.
notes.explanation: It batch-runs pipelines defined with the Kubeflow Pipelines or TensorFlow Extended frameworks.
notes.example: Like a recipe card a kitchen follows the same way every time: the same steps run in the same order whenever you start it.
notes.evidence: Agent Platform Pipelines lets you automate, monitor, and govern your machine learning (ML) systems in a serverless manner by using ML pipelines to orchestrate your ML workflows. You can batch run ML pipelines defined using the Kubeflow Pipelines or the TensorFlow Extended (TFX) framework.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Introduction to Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Pipelines, “Introduction to Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Pipelines”

notes.front: What is Model Garden?
notes.back: A library of AI models in Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform for discovering, testing, customising and deploying models and assets.
notes.explanation: Its models and assets come from Google and from Google’s partners.
notes.example: Like a garden centre for models: you browse, try a few, adapt one, and have it planted for you.
notes.evidence: Model Garden is an AI/ML model library that helps you discover, test, customize, and deploy models and assets from Google and Google partners.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Overview of Model Garden (Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform), “Overview of Model Garden”

notes.front: What is Gemini Enterprise?
notes.back: An intranet search, AI assistant and agentic platform that draws on data sources from across an organisation.
notes.explanation: Prebuilt connectors bring in third-party applications such as Confluence, Jira and Microsoft SharePoint.
notes.example: Like a company librarian who can search every team’s shelves and also run errands for you.
notes.evidence: Gemini Enterprise is an intranet search, AI assistant, and agentic platform. It empowers knowledge workers with generative AI and agentic workflows by leveraging data sources from across your organization. Gemini Enterprise includes prebuilt connectors for commonly-used third-party applications like Confluence, Jira, Microsoft SharePoint, and ServiceNow.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, What is Gemini Enterprise?, “What is Gemini Enterprise?”

notes.front: What is NotebookLM Enterprise, which Google Cloud documentation now calls Gemini Notebook Enterprise?
notes.back: The compliant, enterprise-ready version of Google’s notebook tool for researching and writing from sources you supply.
notes.explanation: You add sources such as PDFs, Google Docs and website URLs to a notebook, and its answers are drawn from them.
notes.example: Like a research assistant who reads only the folder you hand over and answers from it.
notes.evidence: Gemini Notebook Enterprise is a highly compliant, enterprise-ready version of Gemini Notebook. Gemini Notebook is an AI-powered research and writing tool that helps you summarize and extract information across dense and complex sources. You do this by adding data sources, such as PDFs, Google Docs, Google Slides, and website URLs, to build a notebook.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, What is Gemini Notebook Enterprise?, “What is Gemini Notebook Enterprise?”

notes.front: What is Gemini Cloud Assist?
notes.back: An AI-powered collaborator built into Google Cloud that gives agentic guidance for designing, deploying, troubleshooting and optimising workloads.
notes.explanation: Its aim is to move you from reactive troubleshooting to proactive, autonomous cloud operations; the documentation labels it a Preview offering.
notes.example: Like a senior colleague sitting in the console who can read your project’s logs and suggest the next step.
notes.evidence: Gemini Cloud Assist serves as your AI-powered collaborator, helping you move from reactive troubleshooting to proactive, autonomous cloud operations. By integrating deeply into the cloud platform, Gemini Cloud Assist simplifies the end-to-end application lifecycle, offering intelligent, agentic guidance for designing, deploying, troubleshooting, and optimizing your workloads.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Gemini Cloud Assist overview, “Gemini Cloud Assist overview”

notes.front: What is the Cloud Vision API?
notes.back: A Google Cloud API of ready-made image-analysis features, such as detecting and extracting the text in an image.
notes.explanation: Its text detection recognises text in an image and converts it to machine-coded text.
notes.example: Like a sharp-eyed assistant who reads the sign in your holiday photo and says what else is in the picture.
notes.evidence: Optical character recognition (OCR) for an image; text recognition and conversion to machine-coded text. Identifies and extracts UTF-8 text in an image.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Features list (Cloud Vision API), “Text detection”

notes.front: What is Speech-to-Text?
notes.back: Google Cloud’s speech recognition service, with three main methods of recognising speech in audio data.
notes.explanation: The simplest method, synchronous recognition, returns results after all the audio has been processed.
notes.example: Like a stenographer who types up what is said in a recording.
notes.evidence: Cloud STT has three main methods to perform speech recognition: Synchronous recognition (REST and gRPC) sends audio data to the Cloud Speech-to-Text API, performs recognition on that data, and returns results after all audio has been processed.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Cloud Speech-to-Text overview, “Speech requests”

notes.front: What is the Video Intelligence API, and what is its status in 2026?
notes.back: A Google Cloud API for analysing video; it has been officially deprecated since 14 September 2026.
notes.explanation: It can still be used until 14 September 2027, when it shuts down, and Google recommends migrating to Gemini models.
notes.example: Like a film archivist who logs what appears in each scene of the footage.
notes.evidence: Starting on September 14, 2026, Video Intelligence API is officially deprecated and will no longer be supported. You can continue using Video Intelligence API until September 14, 2027, when it will be shut down. We recommend migrating to Gemini family of models.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Features (Video Intelligence API), “Features”

notes.front: What is the Natural Language API?
notes.back: A Google Cloud API whose methods analyse and annotate text.
notes.explanation: Each method is a different level of analysis, and each adds information for understanding the language.
notes.example: Like an editor who reads a customer review and tells you whether it is cross and what it is about.
notes.evidence: The Natural Language API has several methods for performing analysis and annotation on your text. Each level of analysis provides valuable information for language understanding.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Natural Language API Basics, “Natural Language features”

notes.front: What is Model Armor?
notes.back: A Google Cloud service that screens the prompts sent to large language models and the responses they return, to make AI applications safer.
notes.explanation: The screening is proactive, to protect against various risks and support responsible AI practices.
notes.example: Like a security guard who checks both the letters going into a building and the replies coming out.
notes.evidence: Model Armor is a Google Cloud service designed to enhance the security and safety of your AI applications. It works by proactively screening LLM prompts and responses, protecting against various risks and ensuring responsible AI practices.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Model Armor overview, “Model Armor overview”

notes.front: On Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, what supplies source data for training, and when is it required?
notes.back: Managed datasets: required for AutoML, optional for custom training.
notes.explanation: Datasets can be created for different data types, including image and tabular data.
notes.evidence: Agent Platform provides managed datasets to simplify this process. Managed datasets allow you to provide source data for training models. They are required for AutoML and optional for custom training. You can create datasets for different data types, including image and tabular data.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Introduction to machine learning on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, “Data preparation”

notes.front: What are two benefits of serverless training on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform?
notes.back: Fully managed compute, with no servers to provision; and multi-node distributed training to reduce time and cost.
notes.explanation: Optimised training jobs for higher performance are another benefit on the list.
notes.evidence: Key benefits of serverless training include: Fully managed compute infrastructure: Train models without provisioning or managing servers. High performance: Optimized training jobs that can provide faster performance. Distributed training: Support for multi-node distributed training to reduce time and cost.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Introduction to machine learning on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, “Model training”

notes.front: Where do you manage a trained model’s lifecycle on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform?
notes.back: In the Model Registry, a central repository for tracking versions, evaluating quality and deploying models to serve inferences.
notes.explanation: Model management is the step after training in the platform’s machine learning workflow.
notes.evidence: After training your model, you can manage it in the Model Registry. The Model Registry is a central repository where you can manage the lifecycle of your ML models. It allows you to track model versions, evaluate model quality, and deploy models for serving inferences.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Introduction to machine learning on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, “Model management”

notes.front: In Agent Platform Pipelines, what is a machine learning pipeline?
notes.back: A portable, extensible description of a workflow as a series of steps called pipeline tasks.
notes.explanation: Each task performs one specific step in training and deploying a model.
notes.evidence: An ML pipeline is a portable and extensible description of an MLOps workflow as a series of steps called pipeline tasks. Each task performs a specific step in the workflow to train and deploy an ML model.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Introduction to Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Pipelines, “What is an ML pipeline?”

notes.front: By default, tasks in an Agent Platform Pipelines pipeline run {{c1::in parallel}}.
notes.explanation: To make tasks run one after another, you link them so that they execute in series.
notes.evidence: By default, pipeline tasks run in parallel. You can link the tasks to execute them in series.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Introduction to Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Pipelines, “Structure of an ML pipeline”

notes.front: How can you run the same Agent Platform Pipelines definition on a recurring basis?
notes.back: Use the scheduler to create recurring pipeline runs from the same definition.
notes.explanation: Each run is an execution instance of the definition; you can also create one-off runs or clone an existing run.
notes.evidence: The execution instance of a pipeline definition is called a pipeline run. You can create a one-time occurrence of a pipeline run or use the scheduler API to create recurring pipeline runs from the same ML pipeline definition. You can also clone an existing pipeline run.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Introduction to Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Pipelines, “Lifecycle of an ML pipeline”

notes.front: What does the lineage of a machine learning artifact from a pipeline run include?
notes.back: All the factors that contributed to its creation, with metadata and references to artifacts derived from it.
notes.explanation: Lineage graphs help you analyse root causes upstream and impact downstream.
notes.evidence: The lineage of an ML artifact includes all the factors that contributed to its creation, along with metadata and references to artifacts derived from it. Lineage graphs help you analyze upstream root cause and downstream impact.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Introduction to Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Pipelines, “Track the lineage of ML artifacts”

notes.front: What are the three model categories in Model Garden?
notes.back: Foundation models, fine-tunable models and task-specific solutions.
notes.explanation: Foundation models are pretrained multitask large models that can be tuned or customised for specific tasks.
notes.evidence: The model categories available in Model Garden are: Category Description Foundation models Pretrained multitask large models that can be tuned or customized for specific tasks
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Overview of Model Garden (Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform), “Explore models”

notes.front: In Model Garden, what happens to a Hugging Face model that the security scans deem unsafe?
notes.back: Hugging Face flags it, and it is blocked from deployment in Model Garden.
notes.explanation: Suspicious models are only marked and can still be deployed, so Google recommends a thorough review before deploying one.
notes.evidence: Models deemed unsafe from these scans are flagged by HuggingFace and blocked from deployment in Model Garden. Models deemed suspicious or those that have the ability to potentially execute remote code are indicated in Model Garden but can still be deployed. We recommend you perform a thorough review of any suspicious model before deploying it within Model Garden.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Overview of Model Garden (Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform), “Model security scanning”

notes.front: How can an organisation restrict which Model Garden models its teams may use?
notes.back: Set a Model Garden organisation policy at the organisation, folder or project level.
notes.explanation: The policy can, for example, allow only models you have vetted and deny all others.
notes.evidence: You can set a Model Garden organization policy at the organization, folder, or project level to control access to specific models in Model Garden. For example, you can allow access to specific models that you've vetted and deny access to all others.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Overview of Model Garden (Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform), “Control access to specific models”

notes.front: For open-source models in Model Garden, how is model tuning charged?
notes.back: For the compute resources used, at the same rate as custom training.
notes.explanation: Deploying the model is likewise charged for the compute resources behind its endpoint.
notes.evidence: Model tuning: You are charged for the compute resources used at the same rate as custom training. See custom training pricing. Model deployment: You are charged for the compute resources used to deploy the model to an endpoint.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Overview of Model Garden (Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform), “Pricing”

notes.front: Which three components does AI Hypercomputer vertically integrate?
notes.back: Performance-optimised infrastructure, open software and consumption options.
notes.explanation: Integrating them aims to maximise goodput, the measure of actual machine learning productivity.
notes.evidence: AI Hypercomputer vertically integrates these three components to maximize goodput—the measure of actual machine learning productivity: Performance-optimized infrastructure: provides accelerators (NVIDIA GPUs and Google Cloud TPUs), networking, and storage resources.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, AI Hypercomputer overview, “System architecture”

notes.front: Which AI Hypercomputer consumption option provisions entire blocks of interconnected nodes atomically for large-scale training?
notes.back: Dynamic Workload Scheduler.
notes.explanation: The other consumption options are flex-start VMs, Spot VMs and reservations, for different workloads.
notes.evidence: Consumption options: offers flexible provisioning options based on your workload needs: Flex-start VMs, Spot VMs, and Reservations: provide flexible options for different workloads. Dynamic Workload Scheduler: provides atomic provisioning for entire blocks of interconnected nodes for large-scale training.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, AI Hypercomputer overview, “System architecture”

notes.front: What are two ways AI Hypercomputer offers to deploy and manage accelerators?
notes.back: Google Kubernetes Engine for automated container-native scaling; and Slurm through Cluster Director.
notes.explanation: Cluster Toolkit blueprints are a third option on the list.
notes.evidence: To deploy and manage your accelerators, you can choose from the following options: Google Kubernetes Engine for automated container-native scaling Slurm through Cluster Director Cluster Toolkit blueprints
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, AI Hypercomputer overview, “System architecture”

notes.front: TPUs can be connected in groups called {{c1::slices}}, which scale up workloads with little to no code changes.
notes.explanation: On-chip high-bandwidth memory also lets TPUs take larger models and batch sizes.
notes.evidence: TPUs have on-chip high-bandwidth memory (HBM) letting you use larger models and batch sizes. TPUs can be connected in groups called slices that scale up your workloads with little to no code changes.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Introduction to Cloud TPU, “Introduction to Cloud TPU”

notes.front: What must compile code that runs on TPUs?
notes.back: The accelerated linear algebra compiler, a just-in-time compiler.
notes.explanation: It takes the graph from the machine learning framework and compiles its linear algebra, loss and gradient parts into TPU machine code.
notes.evidence: Code that runs on TPUs must be compiled by the accelerated linear algebra (XLA) compiler. XLA is a just-in-time compiler that takes the graph emitted by an ML framework application and compiles the linear algebra, loss, and gradient components of the graph into TPU machine code.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Introduction to Cloud TPU, “Introduction to Cloud TPU”

notes.front: What are two kinds of workload that Cloud TPUs are not suited to?
notes.back: Workloads that need high-precision arithmetic; and linear algebra programs that need frequent branching.
notes.explanation: Neural network workloads with custom operations in the main training loop are a third poor fit.
notes.evidence: Cloud TPUs are not suited to the following workloads: Linear algebra programs that require frequent branching or contain many element-wise algebra operations Workloads that require high-precision arithmetic Neural network workloads that contain custom operations in the main training loop
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Introduction to Cloud TPU, “When to use TPUs”

notes.front: Why is a model whose tensors have dynamic shapes not well suited to TPUs?
notes.back: The graph is compiled just in time for the first batch, and later batches with different shapes don’t work.
notes.explanation: Recompiling the graph every time the shape changes would be too slow.
notes.evidence: The XLA compiler compiles an ML graph just in time for the first batch. If any subsequent batches have different shapes, the model doesn't work. (Re-compiling the graph every time the shape changes is too slow.)
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Introduction to Cloud TPU, “Shapes”

notes.front: Through which three Google Cloud services can you use TPUs?
notes.back: Compute Engine, Google Kubernetes Engine and Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.
notes.explanation: The same section notes that the separate Cloud TPU programming interface is deprecated.
notes.evidence: You can use TPUs through Compute Engine, Google Kubernetes Engine, and Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. The Cloud TPU API is deprecated.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Introduction to Cloud TPU, “TPUs in Google Cloud”

notes.front: According to the Cloud TPU guide, which hardware suits quick prototyping that needs maximum flexibility?
notes.back: CPUs.
notes.explanation: Simple models that don’t take long to train, and small models with small effective batch sizes, also point to CPUs.
notes.evidence: Quick prototyping that requires maximum flexibility Simple models that don't take long to train Small models with small, effective batch sizes
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Introduction to Cloud TPU, “When to use TPUs: CPUs”

notes.front: For which kinds of workload are accelerator-optimised G series machine types designed?
notes.back: Graphics-intensive applications, video transcoding and virtual desktops, among others such as simulation.
notes.explanation: The G series can also train smaller models and serve single-host inference.
notes.evidence: Accelerator-optimized G series machine types are designed for workloads such as NVIDIA Omniverse simulation workloads, graphics-intensive applications, video transcoding, and virtual desktops. These machine types support NVIDIA RTX Virtual Workstations (vWS). The G series can also be used for training smaller models and for single-host inference.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, GPU machine types (Compute Engine), “Overview”

notes.front: Which accelerator-optimised machine types are ideal for pre-training and fine-tuning foundation models on large clusters of accelerators?
notes.back: The later-generation A series.
notes.explanation: The A series as a whole is designed for high performance computing, AI and machine learning; an earlier generation suits smaller models and single-host inference.
notes.evidence: Accelerator-optimized A series machine types are designed for high performance computing (HPC), artificial intelligence (AI), and machine learning (ML) workloads. The later generation A series are ideal for pre-training and fine-tuning foundation models that involves large clusters of accelerators, while the A2 series can be used for training smaller models and single host inference.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, GPU machine types (Compute Engine), “Overview”

notes.front: On accelerator-optimised machine types, the GPU model is {{c1::attached to the instance automatically}}.
notes.explanation: On the general-purpose series that allows GPUs, you attach a model from a select set yourself instead.
notes.evidence: For these machine types, the GPU model is automatically attached to the instance. For N1 general-purpose machine types, except for the N1 shared-core (f1-micro and g1-small), you can attach a select set of GPU models.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, GPU machine types (Compute Engine), “Overview”

notes.front: What access rule does Gemini Enterprise apply to the search results and generated answers it gives each person?
notes.back: Access control: each person sees only results and answers drawn from information they are permitted to access.
notes.explanation: It also streamlines agentic workflows, so people need not switch between several AI assistants and agent applications.
notes.evidence: Enforce access-controlled search results and generative answers at scale. Streamline agentic workflows and eliminate the need to switch between multiple AI assistants and agent applications.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, What is Gemini Enterprise?, “Why use Gemini Enterprise?”

notes.front: Where does Gemini Enterprise offer out-of-the-box agents?
notes.back: In the Agent Gallery.
notes.explanation: You can also create and configure your own AI assistants that answer from enterprise or public data.
notes.evidence: Create and configure AI assistants offering generative answers from enterprise or public data. Use out-of-the-box agents, available to you in the Agent Gallery.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, What is Gemini Enterprise?, “Why use Gemini Enterprise?”

notes.front: Where does NotebookLM Enterprise (now called Gemini Notebook Enterprise) keep your data, and can it be shared externally?
notes.back: Always within your Google Cloud project, and it can’t be shared externally.
notes.explanation: The product runs in a Cloud-compliant environment.
notes.evidence: Gemini Notebook Enterprise runs in a Cloud-compliant environment. Your data is always within your Google Cloud project and can't be shared externally.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, What is Gemini Notebook Enterprise?, “Enterprise grade for notebooks”

notes.front: Which Gemini Cloud Assist feature diagnoses complex issues from logs, errors or natural-language prompts?
notes.back: Investigations.
notes.explanation: It can take in logs, metrics and configurations and explore several hypotheses in parallel to trace root causes.
notes.evidence: Investigations. Diagnose complex issues by creating and managing AI-driven investigations based on logs, errors, or natural language prompts. Acting as a user-guided site reliability engineer (SRE), Gemini Cloud Assist can ingest logs, metrics, and configurations to explore multiple hypotheses in parallel and trace root causes across multi-tier topologies.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Gemini Cloud Assist overview, “Support and troubleshoot”

notes.front: Where does Gemini Cloud Assist let you design, configure and provision cloud architectures in natural language?
notes.back: In the Application Design Center.
notes.explanation: It can also generate or refine command-line commands, kubectl manifests and Terraform code for infrastructure.
notes.evidence: Natural language design. Design, configure, provision, and manage complex cloud architectures using natural language interaction within the Application Design Center. Infrastructure as code (IaC). Iteratively generate or refine Google Cloud CLI commands, `kubectl` manifests, and Terraform code for infrastructure and organizational policies
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Gemini Cloud Assist overview, “Design and build”

notes.front: What does Gemini Cloud Assist’s proactive cost anomaly analysis identify?
notes.back: The infrastructure changes that caused a cost spike, and who was responsible for those changes.
notes.explanation: The analysis runs once a day when an anomaly is detected in a project.
notes.evidence: This analysis runs once a day when an anomaly is detected in a project. The agent analyzes the cost spike, analyzes products, SKUs, and resources to identify the infrastructure changes that caused the cost spike along with the user / service account responsible for those changes.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Gemini Cloud Assist overview, “Optimize”

notes.front: What does Google recommend doing with output from Gemini for Google Cloud products?
notes.back: Validate all of it before you use it.
notes.explanation: As an early-stage technology, these products can produce output that seems plausible but is factually incorrect.
notes.evidence: As an early-stage technology, Gemini for Google Cloud products can generate output that seems plausible but is factually incorrect. We recommend that you validate all output from Gemini for Google Cloud products before you use it.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Gemini Cloud Assist overview, “Gemini Cloud Assist overview”

notes.front: Which Cloud Vision API feature is optimised for sparse areas of text within a larger image?
notes.back: Text detection.
notes.explanation: It identifies and extracts the text it finds and converts it to machine-coded text.
notes.evidence: Optical character recognition (OCR) for an image; text recognition and conversion to machine-coded text. Identifies and extracts UTF-8 text in an image. Images: Optimized for sparse areas of text within a larger image.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Features list (Cloud Vision API), “Text detection”

notes.front: Does Cloud Vision API face detection recognise specific individuals?
notes.back: No. Recognition of specific individuals is not supported.
notes.explanation: Face detection rates likelihoods instead, on a six-value scale from very unlikely to very likely.
notes.evidence: Likelihoods ratings are expressed as 6 different values: UNKNOWN, VERY_UNLIKELY, UNLIKELY, POSSIBLE, LIKELY, or VERY_LIKELY. Specific individual Facial Recognition is not supported.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Features list (Cloud Vision API), “Face detection”

notes.front: Which Cloud Vision API feature rates how likely an image is to contain adult, violent or racy content?
notes.back: Explicit content detection (SafeSearch).
notes.explanation: It also gives likelihood ratings for spoof and medical content.
notes.evidence: Provides likelihood ratings for the following explicit content categories: adult, spoof, medical, violence, and racy.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Features list (Cloud Vision API), “Explicit content detection (SafeSearch)”

notes.front: What is the longest audio a synchronous Speech-to-Text request accepts?
notes.back: 1 minute.
notes.explanation: A synchronous request returns results only after all the audio has been processed.
notes.evidence: Synchronous recognition (REST and gRPC) sends audio data to the Cloud Speech-to-Text API, performs recognition on that data, and returns results after all audio has been processed. Synchronous recognition requests are limited to audio data of 1 minute or less in duration.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Cloud Speech-to-Text overview, “Speech requests”

notes.front: Which Speech-to-Text method handles audio of any duration up to 480 minutes?
notes.back: Asynchronous recognition.
notes.explanation: It starts a long-running operation that you poll periodically for the results.
notes.evidence: Asynchronous Recognition (REST and gRPC) sends audio data to the Cloud Speech-to-Text API and initiates a Long-Running Operation. Using this operation, you can periodically poll for recognition results. Use asynchronous requests for audio data of any duration up to 480 minutes.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Cloud Speech-to-Text overview, “Speech requests”

notes.front: Which Natural Language API analysis identifies a writer’s attitude as positive, negative or neutral?
notes.back: Sentiment analysis, through the analyzeSentiment method.
notes.explanation: It looks for the prevailing emotional opinion within the text.
notes.evidence: Sentiment analysis inspects the given text and identifies the prevailing emotional opinion within the text, especially to determine a writer's attitude as positive, negative, or neutral. Sentiment analysis is performed through the analyzeSentiment method.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Natural Language API Basics, “Natural Language features”

notes.front: Which Natural Language API analysis finds known entities in text and the writer’s attitude toward each one?
notes.back: Entity sentiment analysis, through the analyzeEntitySentiment method.
notes.explanation: It joins entity analysis to sentiment, so each proper or common noun gets its own positive, negative or neutral reading.
notes.evidence: Entity sentiment analysis inspects the given text for known entities (proper nouns and common nouns), returns information about those entities, and identifies the prevailing emotional opinion of the entity within the text, especially to determine a writer's attitude toward the entity as positive, negative, or neutral.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Natural Language API Basics, “Natural Language features”

notes.front: Which Natural Language API method returns a content category for a piece of text?
notes.back: Content classification, through the classifyText method.
notes.explanation: Syntactic analysis is a different method: it breaks text into sentences and tokens for further analysis.
notes.evidence: Syntactic analysis extracts linguistic information, breaking up the given text into a series of sentences and tokens (generally, word boundaries), providing further analysis on those tokens. Syntactic Analysis is performed with the analyzeSyntax method. Content classification analyzes text content and returns a content category for the content.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Natural Language API Basics, “Natural Language features”

notes.front: Each Natural Language API call {{c1::detects and returns the language}} of the text if the caller doesn’t specify one.
notes.explanation: The annotateText request can also run sentiment and entity analysis together in one call.
notes.evidence: Each API call also detects and returns the language, if a language is not specified by the caller in the initial request. Additionally, if you wish to perform several natural language operations on given text using only one API call, the annotateText request can also be used to perform sentiment analysis and entity analysis.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Natural Language API Basics, “Natural Language features”

notes.front: Does Model Armor screen prompts, responses or both?
notes.back: Both: the input prompts and the output responses.
notes.explanation: Screening both keeps the model from being exposed to, or generating, malicious or sensitive content.
notes.evidence: Model Armor filters both input (prompts) and output (responses) to prevent the LLM from exposure to or generation of malicious or sensitive content.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Model Armor overview, “Architecture”

notes.front: What must you create to reach Model Armor regional endpoints from inside a VPC network?
notes.back: A Private Service Connect endpoint to the Model Armor APIs.
notes.explanation: Without it, access through Private Google Access or VPC Service Controls can run into certificate errors.
notes.evidence: To access Model Armor regional endpoints from within a VPC network, you must create a Private Service Connect endpoint to the Model Armor APIs. This is required to prevent certificate errors when regional endpoints are accessed using Private Google Access or VPC Service Controls.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Model Armor overview, “Network requirements”

notes.front: Which Model Armor filter guards against commands hidden in a prompt to trick the model into ignoring its instructions?
notes.back: Prompt injection and jailbreak detection.
notes.explanation: Such hidden commands can also make a model reveal sensitive information or act in ways it wasn’t designed to.
notes.evidence: Prompt injection is a security vulnerability where attackers craft special commands within the text input (the prompt) to trick an AI model. This can make the AI ignore its usual instructions, reveal sensitive information, or perform actions it wasn't designed to do.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Model Armor overview, “Prompt injection and jailbreak detection”

notes.front: Which service, used within Model Armor, can transform, tokenise and redact sensitive elements while keeping non-sensitive context?
notes.back: Sensitive Data Protection.
notes.explanation: It aims to reduce the risk of data leaking into and out of AI workloads.
notes.evidence: Sensitive Data Protection can identify sensitive elements, context, and documents to help you reduce the risk of data leakage going into and out of AI workloads. You can use Sensitive Data Protection directly within Model Armor to transform, tokenize, and redact sensitive elements while retaining non-sensitive context.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Model Armor overview, “Sensitive Data Protection”

notes.front: Which responsible AI safety category in Model Armor is applied by default and cannot be turned off?
notes.back: The category for references to child sexual abuse material.
notes.explanation: It sits in the responsible AI safety filter beside categories such as dangerous content.
notes.evidence: Dangerous content Promotes or enables access to harmful goods, services, and activities. CSAM Contains references to child sexual abuse material (CSAM). This filter is applied by default and cannot be turned off.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Model Armor overview, “Responsible AI safety filter”

notes.front: When Model Armor checks prompts and responses for malicious URLs, how many URLs does it scan?
notes.back: Only the first 256 URLs it finds.
notes.explanation: Extraction stops at 256 URLs or at the end of the payload, whichever comes first.
notes.evidence: Model Armor extracts URLs until it reaches 256 URLs or the end of the payload, and scans only the first 256 URLs found in prompts and responses.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Model Armor overview, “Malicious URL detection”

notes.front: Which Model Armor enforcement type logs violations without stopping the request or response?
notes.back: Inspect only.
notes.explanation: It suits testing new policies, gauging likely violation rates and auditing without affecting live traffic.
notes.evidence: If a violation is found, it logs the details to Cloud Logging for monitoring and analysis. However, it doesn't stop the request or response from being processed by the integrated service. This is useful for testing new policies, understanding potential violation rates, and auditing without affecting live traffic.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Model Armor overview, “Define the enforcement type”

notes.front: A team wants the same prepare, train, evaluate and deploy workflow to run every Monday without anyone starting it, with serverless execution. What should it use?
notes.back: A: Agent Platform Pipelines with a scheduled run.
notes.choices:
A) Agent Platform Pipelines with a scheduled run
B) Model Garden
C) Gemini Cloud Assist investigations
D) Migration Center
notes.choicesExplained: B) Model Garden is a library for finding and deploying models, not for orchestrating a workflow. C) Investigations diagnose problems; they don’t run workflows. D) Migration Center plans migrations to Google Cloud.
notes.explanation: A pipeline definition can be run on a recurring basis through the scheduler.
notes.evidence: You can create a one-time occurrence of a pipeline run or use the scheduler API to create recurring pipeline runs from the same ML pipeline definition.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Introduction to Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Pipelines, “Lifecycle of an ML pipeline”

notes.front: A team wants to find an open model from a Google partner, test it and deploy it on Google Cloud, without building its own serving set-up. Where should it start?
notes.back: B: Model Garden.
notes.choices:
A) Agent Platform Pipelines
B) Model Garden
C) NotebookLM Enterprise
D) Cloud Vision API
notes.choicesExplained: A) Pipelines orchestrate workflows; they are not a catalogue of models. C) NotebookLM Enterprise answers from documents you add. D) The Cloud Vision API offers fixed image features, not a choice of models.
notes.explanation: Model Garden is the library for discovering, testing, customising and deploying models from Google and its partners.
notes.evidence: Model Garden is an AI/ML model library that helps you discover, test, customize, and deploy models and assets from Google and Google partners.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Overview of Model Garden (Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform), “Overview of Model Garden”

notes.front: A company’s large training job needs a whole block of interconnected accelerator nodes provisioned together or not at all. Which AI Hypercomputer option fits?
notes.back: A: Dynamic Workload Scheduler.
notes.choices:
A) Dynamic Workload Scheduler
B) Spot VMs
C) Shared-core machine types
D) Cloud Run
notes.choicesExplained: B) Spot VMs are a flexible option, not atomic provisioning of node blocks. C) Shared-core machine types are small general-purpose machines. D) Cloud Run is not among AI Hypercomputer’s consumption options.
notes.explanation: Dynamic Workload Scheduler provides atomic provisioning of entire blocks of interconnected nodes for large-scale training.
notes.evidence: Dynamic Workload Scheduler: provides atomic provisioning for entire blocks of interconnected nodes for large-scale training.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, AI Hypercomputer overview, “System architecture”

notes.front: A ranking model with ultra-large embeddings is dominated by matrix computations, has no custom operations in its training loop and will train for weeks. Which hardware does the Cloud TPU guide point to?
notes.back: C: TPUs.
notes.choices:
A) CPUs
B) GPUs
C) TPUs
D) Shared-core machine types
notes.choicesExplained: A) CPUs suit quick prototyping and small, quick-to-train models. B) GPUs are suggested for models with many custom operations that must partly run on CPUs, which this model lacks. D) Shared-core machine types have no accelerators.
notes.explanation: Matrix-heavy models, weeks-long training and ultra-large embeddings are all on the guide’s list for TPUs.
notes.evidence: Models dominated by matrix computations Models with no custom PyTorch/JAX operations inside the main training loop Models that train for weeks or months Large models with large effective batch sizes Models with ultra-large embeddings common in advanced ranking and recommendation workloads
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Introduction to Cloud TPU, “When to use TPUs”

notes.front: A media firm needs Compute Engine instances with GPUs for video transcoding and virtual desktops. Which machine types are designed for this?
notes.back: C: accelerator-optimised G series.
notes.choices:
A) Later-generation A series
B) TPU slices
C) Accelerator-optimised G series
D) Shared-core machine types
notes.choicesExplained: A) The later A series targets pre-training and fine-tuning foundation models on large clusters. B) TPUs accelerate machine learning, not transcoding or desktops. D) Shared-core machine types have no GPUs.
notes.explanation: The G series is designed for graphics-intensive applications, video transcoding and virtual desktops.
notes.evidence: Accelerator-optimized G series machine types are designed for workloads such as NVIDIA Omniverse simulation workloads, graphics-intensive applications, video transcoding, and virtual desktops.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, GPU machine types (Compute Engine), “Overview”

notes.front: Analysts want an AI tool that answers questions from a set of reports they upload themselves, with the data kept in the company’s Google Cloud project. Which product fits best?
notes.back: C: NotebookLM Enterprise.
notes.choices:
A) Gemini Cloud Assist
B) Natural Language API
C) NotebookLM Enterprise
D) Model Armor
notes.choicesExplained: A) Gemini Cloud Assist helps design and run cloud workloads, not research uploaded reports. B) The Natural Language API annotates text but doesn’t answer questions from a notebook. D) Model Armor screens prompts and responses.
notes.explanation: NotebookLM Enterprise builds a notebook from sources you add and grounds its answers in them.
notes.evidence: You do this by adding data sources, such as PDFs, Google Docs, Google Slides, and website URLs, to build a notebook. The AI grounds its responses in these documents.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, What is Gemini Notebook Enterprise?, “What is Gemini Notebook Enterprise?”

notes.front: Staff want one search across Confluence, Jira and SharePoint that only shows each person what they are allowed to see. Which product fits?
notes.back: C: Gemini Enterprise.
notes.choices:
A) Model Garden
B) Gemini Cloud Assist
C) Gemini Enterprise
D) Speech-to-Text
notes.choicesExplained: B) Gemini Cloud Assist helps with cloud workloads, not company-wide document search. A) Model Garden is a model library. D) Speech-to-Text recognises speech in audio.
notes.explanation: Gemini Enterprise has prebuilt connectors for such applications and a single search with permissions-aware access.
notes.evidence: Gemini Enterprise includes prebuilt connectors for commonly-used third-party applications like Confluence, Jira, Microsoft SharePoint, and ServiceNow. This provides employees with a single, multimodal search interface offering permissions-aware access to enterprise information.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, What is Gemini Enterprise?, “What is Gemini Enterprise?”

notes.front: An on-call engineer wants AI help to trace the root cause of recurring errors from the service’s logs, metrics and configuration. What should they use?
notes.back: C: a Gemini Cloud Assist investigation.
notes.choices:
A) Model Armor
B) Gemini Enterprise’s Agent Gallery
C) A Gemini Cloud Assist investigation
D) Natural Language API syntactic analysis
notes.choicesExplained: A) Model Armor screens model prompts and responses. B) The Agent Gallery offers workplace agents, not cloud troubleshooting. D) Syntactic analysis breaks text into sentences and tokens; it finds no root causes.
notes.explanation: Investigations take in logs, metrics and configurations to trace root causes.
notes.evidence: Acting as a user-guided site reliability engineer (SRE), Gemini Cloud Assist can ingest logs, metrics, and configurations to explore multiple hypotheses in parallel and trace root causes across multi-tier topologies.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Gemini Cloud Assist overview, “Support and troubleshoot”

notes.front: An insurer scans handwritten claim forms and wants the writing turned into text. Which Cloud Vision API feature fits best?
notes.back: C: document text detection.
notes.choices:
A) Label detection
B) Text detection
C) Document text detection
D) Object localisation
notes.choicesExplained: A) Label detection gives general labels for the image, not its text. B) Text detection is optimised for sparse text within a larger image. D) Object localisation labels and boxes objects.
notes.explanation: Document text detection is optimised for images that are documents, with dense text or handwriting.
notes.evidence: Images: Optimized for dense areas of text in an image (images that are documents), and images that contain handwriting.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Features list (Cloud Vision API), “Document text detection (dense text / handwriting)”

notes.front: An events app must show captions from a microphone while the speaker is still talking. Which Speech-to-Text method fits?
notes.back: D: streaming recognition.
notes.choices:
A) Synchronous recognition
B) Asynchronous recognition
C) A batch pipeline in Agent Platform Pipelines
D) Streaming recognition
notes.choicesExplained: A) Synchronous recognition returns results only after all the audio is processed. B) Asynchronous recognition is polled for results later. C) A batch pipeline doesn’t give results while someone is speaking.
notes.explanation: Streaming recognition is designed for real-time purposes and returns interim results while audio is still being captured.
notes.evidence: Streaming requests are designed for real-time recognition purposes, such as capturing live audio from a microphone. Streaming recognition provides interim results while audio is being captured, allowing result to appear, for example, while a user is still speaking.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Cloud Speech-to-Text overview, “Speech requests”

notes.front: A shop wants to know, this week, whether its product reviews are positive, negative or neutral, and has no data scientists to train a model. What fits best?
notes.back: A: the Natural Language API’s sentiment analysis.
notes.choices:
A) The Natural Language API’s sentiment analysis
B) Custom training on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform
C) A TPU slice
D) Video Intelligence API
notes.choicesExplained: B) Custom training means building your own model, which the shop can’t do. C) A TPU slice is hardware for training, not a ready answer. D) The Video Intelligence API analyses video and is deprecated.
notes.explanation: Sentiment analysis is a ready-made method that identifies a writer’s attitude as positive, negative or neutral.
notes.evidence: Sentiment analysis inspects the given text and identifies the prevailing emotional opinion within the text, especially to determine a writer's attitude as positive, negative, or neutral.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Natural Language API Basics, “Natural Language features”

notes.front: A support chatbot must not leak customers’ personal data in prompts to its language model or in the model’s replies. Which service is designed for this?
notes.back: D: Model Armor.
notes.choices:
A) Google Cloud Armor
B) Natural Language API entity analysis
C) A VPC firewall rule
D) Model Armor
notes.choicesExplained: A) Google Cloud Armor protects web applications from network attacks; it doesn’t read model prompts. B) Entity analysis finds named things in text but redacts nothing. C) A firewall rule filters traffic by connection, not by content.
notes.explanation: Reducing the risk of leaking personal information in model prompts or responses is one of Model Armor’s listed use cases.
notes.evidence: Mitigate the risk of leaking sensitive intellectual property (IP) and personally identifiable information (PII) in LLM prompts or responses.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Model Armor overview, “Use cases”

notes.front: How does a pipeline component relate to a pipeline task?
notes.back: A component is the reusable definition of a step; a task is an instantiation of a component with specific inputs.
notes.explanation: You can use predefined Google Cloud Pipeline Components or write your own custom components.
notes.evidence: Components are the basis of defining tasks in an ML pipeline. To define pipeline tasks, you can either use predefined Google Cloud Pipeline Components or create your own custom components.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Introduction to Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Pipelines, “Pipeline component”

notes.front: In AI Hypercomputer, how do general GPUs differ from clustered GPUs?
notes.back: General: independent compute units with asynchronous maintenance. Clustered: one tightly coupled system with synchronised maintenance.
notes.explanation: The split is by how the system handles the GPUs’ lifecycle events and maintenance.
notes.evidence: GPUs: categorized by how the system handles their lifecycle events and maintenance: General GPUs: infrastructure managed as independent compute units with asynchronous maintenance. Clustered GPUs: high-performance clusters managed as a single tightly coupled system with synchronized maintenance.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, AI Hypercomputer overview, “System architecture”

notes.front: Which hardware does the Cloud TPU guide suggest for models with many custom PyTorch operations that must run at least partly on CPUs?
notes.back: GPUs, not TPUs.
notes.explanation: Medium-to-large models with larger effective batch sizes are also on the guide’s list for GPUs.
notes.evidence: Models with a significant number of custom PyTorch/JAX operations that must run at least partially on CPUs Models with TensorFlow ops that are not available on Cloud TPU (see the list of available TensorFlow ops) Medium-to-large models with larger effective batch sizes
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Introduction to Cloud TPU, “When to use TPUs: GPUs”

notes.front: On Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, how does AutoML differ from custom models?
notes.back: AutoML is a fast path to high-quality models; custom models are built with frameworks such as TensorFlow and PyTorch.
notes.explanation: Either way, the platform runs the whole machine learning lifecycle for you.
notes.evidence: Whether you are using AutoML for a fast path to high-quality models or creating custom models with popular frameworks like TensorFlow and PyTorch, Agent Platform operationalizes the entire ML lifecycle.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Introduction to machine learning on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, “Introduction to machine learning on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform”

notes.front: If the Cloud Vision API’s general object localisation is not specific enough for your images, what does the documentation suggest instead?
notes.back: Create a custom machine learning model with AutoML Vision Object Detection.
notes.explanation: A custom model is built for your own specific object detection use case, which ready-made features are not.
notes.evidence: Need customized object detection? With AutoML Vision Object Detection you can create a custom machine learning model for your specific image object detection use case.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Features list (Cloud Vision API), “Object localization”

notes.front: How does notebook sharing differ between the personal notebook product and NotebookLM Enterprise (now called Gemini Notebook Enterprise)?
notes.back: Personal notebooks can be shared publicly or by email link; enterprise notebooks only with users in the same Google Cloud project.
notes.explanation: In both products, a notebook starts out private to its user.
notes.evidence: Notebooks can be shared with viewer or editor permissions; either publicly or by email links with other users. Notebooks are private to the user. They can only be shared to other users within the same Google Cloud project.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, What is Gemini Notebook Enterprise?, “Differences between Gemini Notebook and Gemini Notebook Enterprise”

notes.front: How do Model Armor floor settings differ from Model Armor templates?
notes.back: Templates give flexibility per application; floor settings set minimum requirements for all templates created at project level.
notes.explanation: Floor settings give a baseline level of protection across all of an organisation’s AI applications.
notes.evidence: Although Model Armor templates provide flexibility for individual applications, organizations often need to establish a baseline level of protection across all their AI applications. Use Model Armor floor settings to establish this baseline. They define minimum requirements for all templates created at the project level in the Google Cloud resource hierarchy.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, Model Armor overview, “Model Armor floor settings”
